**Switching Clanker to headless browsers is the biggest saving: about 8× cheaper.** Since Slack isn’t showing a live preview, we’re paying for a visible browser without using that benefit.

1. **Use headless by default:** roughly **$0.06/hour**, so $5 covers about **83 active browser-hours**. We should first verify screenshots and the browser tools work in this mode. [Kernel rates](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/info/pricing)
2. **Disconnect when waiting:** detach the browser connection while waiting for your reply, OTP, or approval. Connected clients prevent free standby. Reconnect when work resumes. [Standby rules](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/browsers/standby)
3. **Close browsers after completion or cancellation:** stop the supervisor and delete the session so connections don’t linger.
4. **Keep visible mode as a fallback:** use it only for flows that fail in headless mode.

The combination matters: **headless lowers the hourly price; disconnecting prevents paying through long waits.** Our actual session charges still need verification.

Start with a headless compatibility check and an audit of when Clanker disconnects.

content.text:
**The main cons are harder human takeover and possible compatibility issues with particular sites.** Headless still loads and renders pages: modern Chrome shares its browser implementation with visible mode and supports screenshots. [Chrome docs](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/automation-and-testing/headless)

For Clanker:

1. **Manual login becomes harder.** If you need to take over for a CAPTCHA, login challenge, or unusual prompt, we may need a separate visible-browser flow. Kernel’s exact headless takeover support needs verification.
2. **Some sites may behave differently.** We should test our actual grocery and travel flows for login failures, challenges, and rendering differences. Headless doesn’t automatically mean blocked, and visible mode doesn’t guarantee acceptance.
3. **Our tools need compatibility checks.** Page-based clicks, typing, and screenshots are a good fit. Anything relying on desktop coordinates, browser menus, or native dialogs may need adaptation.
4. **It doesn’t fix lingering connections.** A connected headless browser still bills; it just bills at a lower rate. Disconnecting during waits remains necessary. [Kernel standby rules](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/browsers/standby)

**My recommendation stays headless by default, with visible mode for verified exceptions.** The tradeoff is worth testing, but we haven’t yet verified Clanker’s flows in headless mode.

I want you to refer to Kernel.sh documentation and tell me how I can save on costs if I'm not using live preview. Does it make any difference? Does it make any difference to use the browser in headful or headless mode? If all I want to do is build browser agent, that is what Clanker is actually.
I’ll check Kernel’s documentation for the price difference and what keeps a browser billable when Live View is closed.

**Yes, headless is 8× cheaper. But simply closing Live Preview doesn’t reduce a headful browser’s hourly rate.**

Kernel bills these as separate browser configurations:

| Mode | Cost per active hour | What $5 covers |
|---|---:|---:|
| Headful | ~$0.48 | ~10.4 hours |
| Headless | ~$0.06 | ~83.3 hours |

Headful uses 8 GB; headless uses 1 GB. You pay for that configuration whether or not you watch it. [Kernel pricing](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/info/pricing)

**When does avoiding Live Preview save money?**

A browser remains billable while **any CDP connection, WebDriver connection, or Live View connection is open**, or a computer-control request is running. Once none are active for five seconds, it enters **free standby**.

So closing Live Preview helps only if the agent’s connections are also disconnected. An agent sitting connected while waiting for your Slack reply still costs money. [Kernel standby documentation](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/browsers/standby)

**For Clanker, I’d revise my earlier blanket recommendation.** Kernel specifically recommends headful for agent workflows on sites with bot detection because it provides better stealth, Live View, and replays. It describes headless as suitable for simple scraping. That doesn’t make headless unsuitable for all agents, but it means grocery, travel, and login flows need testing before switching. [Kernel browser configuration](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/introduction/create)

The practical cost-saving approach is:

1. **Fix connected waiting first.** Clanker starts a persistent CDP supervisor. Disconnect all browser clients during user/OTP/approval waits, then reconnect when work resumes.
2. **Use headless for flows verified to work there.** Start with searches, reading pages, and straightforward DOM automation.
3. **Keep headful for flows needing better stealth or desktop interaction.** Kernel’s computer controls operate at the OS level, including native dialogs; they aren’t interchangeable with page-only automation. [Computer controls](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/browsers/computer-controls)
4. **Delete sessions when tasks finish or are cancelled.** Shortening the idle timeout alone won’t solve billing while a client remains connected.

**For Clanker, connection lifecycle is the first saving to pursue; headless is an additional 87.5% runtime saving wherever compatibility holds.**

Kernel explicitly describes **headful as providing better stealth for agent workflows on sites with bot detection**, while headless uses less memory and suits simpler scraping. Therefore, dropping Live Preview doesn’t establish that headful’s other benefits are unnecessary. [Kernel configuration documentation](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/introduction/create)

For your current usage, my recommendation is:

1. **Keep the authentication flow as it is initially.**
2. **Test headless for the automation browser:** resume the authenticated profile, search Zepto, add an item, and verify the cart without submitting payment.
3. **Compare success and retries with headful.** If the same flow succeeds reliably, headless cuts its runtime price from approximately **$0.48 to $0.06/hour**. [Kernel pricing](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/info/pricing)

**Verified conclusion: you currently use headful, stealth, residential routing, and authentication profiles. Headless equivalence remains untested; platform usage records alone cannot establish it.**

content.text:
**The CLI logs support using headless for Clanker’s main automation, while keeping headful for authentication and human takeover. They don’t justify switching everything unchanged.**

I downloaded **14,590 Kernel audit records for October 8–9** and inspected the latest **100 browser sessions**:

| Actual platform usage | Finding |
|---|---|
| 418 Playwright execution requests | Page automation is a substantial part of your workload. |
| 224 CDP connection requests | Clanker also controls browsers through CDP. |
| 8 OS-level screenshots | Seven came from the Kernel JS SDK on authentication sessions; one came from a browser client. These aren’t evidence that Clanker’s main agent requires desktop screenshots. |
| No recorded computer mouse/keyboard API calls | The audit contains no evidence of reliance on Kernel’s OS-level clicking or typing. CDP actions aren’t individually exposed here. |
| 100 sessions, all headful, 8 GB, no GPU | You’re consistently paying for headful; there’s no headless comparison in this sample. |

Those 100 sessions report **10.11 aggregate active hours**, approximately **$4.85 at headful rates**. The same runtime in headless would cost approximately **$0.61**, assuming equivalent behavior. This is a sample calculation, not a full invoice reconciliation. [Kernel rates](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/info/pricing)

**My recommendation based on the logs:**

1. **Use headless for the main Playwright/CDP automation browser**, after verifying the Zepto flow.
2. **Keep managed authentication and takeover headful initially.** Your logs show those flows using desktop screenshots.
3. **Disconnect CDP during waits.** Headless still bills while connected; free standby requires the connections to close. [Standby rules](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/browsers/standby)

One uncertainty remains: **site acceptance**. Kernel says headful provides better stealth for bot-detected sites. Audit records cannot establish whether Zepto will accept the same authenticated flow headlessly. Historical telemetry returned no events, and Chromium logs were unavailable because the session had ended. [Kernel configuration](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/introduction/create)

**Verified conclusion: the logs show no demonstrated headful requirement for Clanker’s core automation, but authentication and headless site compatibility still need verification.**
